full_judgment:
2. Government of Bangladesh is the appellant. Respondent Abani Kanta Chakraborty instituted the suit for declaration of his tenancy right in respect of the Suit land contending that over one acre of CS Plot No. 3271 was possessed by him for the last 40 years. The suit land is contiguous to his homestead. He grew jute to the knowledge of the original landlord. Since 1940 he acquired tenancy right to the suit land but the suit land has been recorded as khas land of the Government. In 1964 he wanted to pay rent to the Howla Tahsil Kutchery and there for the first time he came to know that in the rent-roll the suit land has been wrongly shown as khas land the Government, thereby casting a cloud on his tenancy right. 

 3. Defendant-appellants contested the suit. Their case was that the suit land is part of CS Plot No. 3271 of mouza Hogla which consists of 21.61 acres of land out of which the plaintiff claimed only one acre. The rent receiving interest of the Zamindars were acquired under Chapter II and the entire CS plot was acquired by the Government as the same was under the khas possession of the ex-landlord. The plaintiff has no possession and the suit is liable to be dismissed The case of defendants No. 2-3 was that they took pattan of 3 acres of land out of the suit Dag No. 3271 and they are in possession on payment of Government rent. H is stated that the plaintiff himself also prayed for taking pattan of a portion of the land but since he was not in possession his prayer was not granted by the Government. 

 7. The arguments are not convicting. Firstly, PO No. 90 of 1972 has no manner of application, because the plaintiff has not challenged the acquisition of any property under the State acquisition and Tenancy Act, nor the question of adverse possession arises here though in framing the suit he took the plea for his tenancy as against the ex-landlord. The plaintiff's simple case is that he was on the land since 1927 and the land was a low land. It silted up gradually and in 1940 it became fit for cultivation of jute and since it was regulated by law, he applied for lisence and got Exhibit 1. Then he grew jute. The landlord was Maharaja Sashi Kanta Acharya Bahadur. It was very much known to the Zamindars that he was in possession. In 1951 with the acquisition of rent receiving interest, the Zamindar has disappeared and he becomes tenant under section 3(4) (e): 

 "all tenants holding lands in such estates, (taluks, tenures, holdings or tenancies) directly under the rent-receiver specified in the notification under sub section (I), shall become tenants directly under the Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate, in respect of the rent paying lands so held by them, to the Government and not to anybody else." 

 8. The plaintiff stated that he went to pay rent to the Tahsil office, but it was not accepted, because it was shown as khas land of the Government. Since he has become a tenant under the law his obligation to pay rent still continues (see section 140 when the arrears of rent shall bear simple interest at the rate of six and a quarter percentum per annum from the expiry of the year in which the rent or installments of rent, as the case may be, fall due to the date of payment of the filing of certificate under the Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 subject to the period of limitation as given by section 142. 

 These circumstances make a fitting story of the plaintiff that he is in possession of the land. Then the acquisition of the rent receiving interest does not affect him at all because being a small cultivator who claimed possession in only 1 acre of land out of 21 acres of the suit plot there is no difficulty to recognize the status as a tenant which he acquired by operation of law. 

 10. In MH Khandakar vs Bangladesh DLR (SC) 1 this Court explained the meaning of 'raiyat' and "tenant" and it was pointed out that a tenant of an agricultural holding is generally called 'raiyat'. Further it was observed that the main object of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was to eliminate all those interests intervening between the Government and the tenant in actual occupation of land to create, throughout the country, one class of tenants directly under the Government, which would be the sole receiver of rent payable by the tenants in rested of the lands comprised in their tenancy and their rights and liabilities would be regulated by uniform code of laws. In the present case the rent-receiving interests were acquired by the Government, since the Zamindar was replaced by the Government. And the tenant, the respondent, intended to pay rent to the Government and went to do so to the Tahsil Office; it was not accepted. But he is on the land-it is only one acre out of 21 acres. He even wanted to take pattan from the Government. His tenancy light has matured over the last forty years to his status. It was only against the ex-landlord that he took the plea of adverse possession as abundant caution. In so far as the Government, his new land- lord, is concerned, he was willing to pay rent and continue to do so. Payment of arrear rent is subject to law. His status however cannot be denied.
